scope: Source-backed operational communications event catalog preserving NASA-reported timing precision, planned-versus-reported distinctions, RF-versus-optical distinctions, and sequence-only evidence without inventing timestamps.

precision_policy.EXACT: Source provides sufficient explicit precision to treat the timestamp as an exact event value.
precision_policy.MINUTE_LEVEL: Source identifies a specific minute. Seconds are represented as zero only as a storage convention and do not imply second-level precision.
precision_policy.APPROXIMATE: Source provides approximate timing such as just after noon or about two hours before another event. Any stored anchor is explicitly non-exact.
precision_policy.DATE_LEVEL: Source establishes the calendar date but does not support a useful time of day.
precision_policy.SEQUENCE_ONLY: Source establishes ordering relative to another event or phase but does not support a timestamp.

event_state_policy.OBSERVED_REPORTED: NASA or NASA/JPL reporting states that the event occurred.
event_state_policy.REPORTED: NASA reports an event or anomaly but without enough evidence to classify it as a precise observed timestamp.
event_state_policy.SEQUENCE_REPORTED: NASA establishes sequence or relative ordering without a defensible event timestamp.

sources.title: Networks Keeping NASA's Artemis II Mission Connected
claims_used: Artemis II used the Near Space Network and Deep Space Network as its primary communications networks.
Primary support transitioned to the Deep Space Network after translunar injection.
O2O was a separate optical communications demonstration.

sources.title: The Deep Space Network Acquires Artemis II Signal
claims_used: Soon after launch, the Near Space Network led communications with Orion before handoff to the Deep Space Network.

sources.title: The Deep Space Network Acquires Artemis II Signal
claims_used: A DSN visualization shows DSS-54 and DSS-56 at Madrid communicating with Artemis II on April 1, 2026.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 3: Crew Prepares for First Correction Burn, Readies to Receive Lunar Observation Assignment
claims_used: NASA planned an Orion emergency communications system test on the Deep Space Network in the second half of the day.
O2O connected with two U.S.-based ground stations and transmitted high-definition video and other mission data.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 3: Crew Prepares Cabin for Lunar Flyby
claims_used: NASA later reported the crew had been testing Orion's emergency communications system in deep space.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 4: Deep-Space Flying, Lunar Flyby Prep
claims_used: Just after 12 p.m. EDT, O2O surpassed 100 gigabytes of data downlinked during the mission.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 6: Crew Ready for Lunar Flyby
claims_used: Mission control expected communications loss at 6:44 p.m. EDT.
Planned Earthset was 6:45 p.m. EDT.
Planned Earthrise was 7:25 p.m. EDT.
Mission control expected communications reacquisition at 7:25 p.m. EDT.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 6: Lunar Flyby Updates
claims_used: NASA reported Earthset at 6:41 p.m. EDT.
NASA reported Orion entered the planned communications blackout at 6:44 p.m. EDT.
NASA reported Earthrise at 7:24 p.m. EDT.
NASA reported DSN reacquisition occurred moments after Earthrise.

sources.title: Artemis II Flight Day 9: Second Return Correction Burn Complete
claims_used: RTC2 occurred at 10:53 p.m. EDT and lasted nine seconds.
About two hours before the burn, an unexpected return-link loss of signal occurred during a data-rate change.
Two-way communications were reestablished shortly afterward.

events.name: Near Space Network leads initial Orion communications
Early mission DSN signal acquisition shown from Madrid
Primary communications support transitions from NSN to DSN
Orion emergency communications system tested in deep space
O2O connects with two U.S. ground stations
Unexpected return-link loss during data-rate change
Two-way communications reestablished after return-link loss

guardrails: Minute-level timestamps do not imply second-level measurement precision.
Approximate anchors are computational reference points and must never be presented as exact event times.
Date-level evidence must not be assigned an invented time of day.
Sequence-only evidence must not be assigned an invented timestamp.
Planned events must remain distinguishable from events reported during or after execution.
Reported Earthset and Earthrise are geometric mission context and are not identical to operational RF LOS or AOS.
The NSN-to-DSN support transition is not assigned an exact handoff time because the public source establishes sequence but not a defensible timestamp.
The Flight Day 9 return-link loss is not assigned an exact 00:53 UTC event time; 00:53 UTC is only the approximate anchor produced by subtracting two hours from RTC2.
O2O optical communications activity must remain distinct from the mission's primary RF communications availability.
The catalog does not infer antenna assignment, link margin, signal strength, network scheduling, or communications performance beyond NASA's public reporting.
